headline: GitLab positions itself as an all-remote, inclusive DevSecOps platform company where everyone can contribute.
identity: GitLab has consistently valued remote work, inclusion, and the belief that everyone can contribute—a mission that has only strengthened over time. The company's language around altruism and belonging surged from 2019 onward (zscore rising from -0.33 to +1.23 by 2022), and inclusion language climbed steadily from 2018 (when explicit DEI mentions first appeared) through 2026. However, craft language—once a core part of the pitch—wavered sharply downward in 2024 (zscore -1.42), suggesting a shift away from emphasizing culture and belonging as a draw. AI mentions remained absent until 2025, then jumped to 12.5% prevalence in 2025 and 25% in 2026, signaling a recent pivot toward positioning GitLab as an AI-era platform.
fit: You might be a good fit if you value autonomy, transparency, and the ability to work asynchronously from anywhere, and if you're drawn to a mission centered on democratizing software creation. The careers copy increasingly emphasizes 'everyone can contribute' and 'show up as your full self,' suggesting GitLab seeks people who thrive in flat, distributed environments and care about inclusive culture—though recent emphasis on AI-powered DevSecOps suggests technical ambition and product innovation matter equally.

sections.heading: The Rise of Inclusion and Belonging (2018–2026)
sections.body:
GitLab's language around diversity, inclusion, and belonging was nearly absent before 2018. Starting in 2018, explicit DEI language entered the careers copy—mentions of #women and #lgbtq Slack channels, transgender medical services, and diverse interview panels. By 2019, the altruism zscore jumped to -0.33 (from -0.90 in 2018), and inclusion language grew from 0.20 to 0.69 zscore. The peak came in 2022, when altruism hit zscore +1.23 and inclusion reached +0.84, with language like 'Diversity, Inclusion, & Belonging is woven into our values and everything we do' and 'a place where anyone can thrive.' This language has remained stable through 2026, suggesting it is now foundational to how GitLab describes itself.

Notably, the shift from explicit demographic language (e.g., 'women,' 'LGBTQ') to aspirational, belonging-focused language occurred around 2021–2022. By 2023, explicit demographic terms had largely disappeared, replaced by broader phrases like 'creating inclusive environments' and 'spaces where everyone belongs.' This mirrors broader industry trends but also suggests GitLab moved from signaling specific demographic support to emphasizing universal belonging.

sections.heading: Remote Work and Autonomy: Consistent but Cooling
sections.body:
All-remote work has been central to GitLab's identity since 2015. Early copy emphasized independence and flexibility ('independence is both valued and required'). By 2019–2021, remote work language peaked in techno-optimism (zscore +0.88 in 2021), with quotes like 'In the future, companies who make digital products are going to be much more all-remote.' Wellbeing language also surged during this period (zscore +1.24 in 2019–2021), emphasizing flexibility to 'be there for other people' and 'spend more time with family.'

However, 2024 marked a sharp reversal. Craft language (which captures culture and belonging messaging) dropped to zscore -1.42, the lowest in the dataset. Techno-optimism also fell to -1.29 in 2024. While remote work remains mentioned, the careers copy shifted away from celebrating it as a lifestyle or cultural advantage. By 2025–2026, remote work language stabilized but no longer dominated the pitch. The emphasis moved toward product capability and AI innovation rather than the freedom and flexibility of distributed work.

sections.heading: AI Emerges as a New Narrative (2025–2026)
sections.body:
AI was entirely absent from GitLab's careers language through 2024. In 2025, AI mentions appeared for the first time, with 12.5% prevalence (2 of 16 chunks). The language was cautious: 'Using AI in the interview process' and 'the most comprehensive AI-powered DevSecOps platform.' By 2026, AI prevalence doubled to 25% (4 of 16 chunks), with more assertive framing: 'the trusted enterprise platform for software creation in the AI era' and 'agentic' capabilities mentioned alongside 'guided by humans.'

This timing is significant. The AI pivot coincides with the 2024 dip in craft and culture language, suggesting GitLab is repositioning from 'a great place to work' to 'a cutting-edge platform for the AI era.' The mission statement evolved from 'everyone can contribute' to 'unlock every team to ship software at the speed of imagination' in the AI era. Notably, the company added language about 'machine scale, guided by humans,' signaling an attempt to balance AI capability with human agency—a tension that may reflect broader industry and candidate concerns.
